title: The Story Is in the Controls: Play One Short Game With a Friend
subtitle: A low-pressure way to notice what a game tells us through its places, sounds, objects and choices—and what changes when we notice together.
imageAlt: Two friends sit side by side on a couch, one holding a game controller while the other points toward a detail on the screen.
imageConcept: Two friends share a couch in a warmly lit living room: one plays a quiet, story-rich game while the other leans in to point out a detail on screen; a second controller rests within reach.
body: Choose a game that gives you room to look

A useful way to share a video game is to treat it less like a test of reflexes and more like a place to explore together. Pick something with a short, natural stopping point: a single chapter, a brief scene, or a small area you can leave without losing a long stretch of progress. Games built around exploration, conversation, or puzzles can work well, but there is no required genre. Choose something neither person has to pretend to enjoy. If one of you already knows the game, agree to explore rather than race ahead; if it is new to both, let the uncertainty be part of the fun. Keep the first session to about 20 or 30 minutes, including time to talk. The point is not to finish a story or prove that games are art. It is to notice how this particular game asks a person to move through, interpret, and respond to its world.
Set the scene before pressing start

Before you play, take a minute to make the setup comfortable for both people. Check whether the screen is easy to see, the sound is at a welcome level, and the controller is comfortable to hold. Look through the game’s available options together: subtitles, text size, remappable controls, difficulty, camera movement, and audio cues may be relevant, but availability varies from game to game. Ask rather than assume what would help, and let each person decide what they want to use. A study of a point-and-click game designed with audio feedback compared how sighted and visually impaired participants experienced its story; the researchers reported that their perceptions were almost identical. That finding belongs to that game and study, not to every game or player, but it is a reminder that design choices can open different ways into a shared story [1]. The practical principle is simple: make room for each person to participate in the way that works for them.
Read the world, not just the dialogue

Once the game begins, look for the story in more than the spoken or written lines. What has been left on a table? Which places seem cared for, abandoned, guarded, or ordinary? Does the music change when you enter a room? Are there repeated colors, signs, sounds, or objects that make the setting feel welcoming or uneasy? You do not need to decode every clue or agree on what it means. A researcher examining games as history lessons describes how world-building, item descriptions, and design can convey historical context, while also cautioning that learning is not guaranteed simply because a game contains history. That is a useful distinction: an object or detail can invite interpretation without proving a single reading [2]. Try an open question instead of a quiz: “What made you notice that?” or “What do you think this place wants us to understand?” Curiosity keeps the conversation grounded in what is actually on screen.
Take turns with the controller and the noticing

For the first stretch, one person can play while the other watches for a detail that might be easy to miss. The observer is not a coach, back-seat driver, or scorekeeper. They can point out something in the environment, ask what a choice might lead to, or simply keep quiet until a natural pause. Then switch roles. If the game permits, the new player can make the next decision; if not, they can take charge of navigation or observation while the first person continues. Both roles count as participation. Public historian Darren Reid notes that games can cede narrative control to players through meaningful choices, a point that can prompt you to notice how taking turns shapes the session [3]. You do not have to make the session perfectly balanced. Just give each person a genuine chance to handle the controller and to shape what the two of you notice.
Ask what the game lets you choose

Choices can reveal the shape of a story, including the limits of a player’s influence. Notice whether you can decide what to say, where to go, whom to help, or what to pick up. Then notice what remains fixed: a locked door, a character who will not answer, a task the game insists you complete. Darren Reid notes that games can cede narrative control to players through meaningful choices [3]. That makes a useful prompt for a shared session: “What can we change here, and what can’t we?” The answer may be practical—the controls allow one route but not another—or interpretive: the game gives you a choice but makes every option feel costly. Keep the distinction clear. The game has established these particular possibilities; you and your friend can discuss their meaning, but you do not have to claim that one playthrough tells the whole story.
Make the conversation welcoming, not competitive

Different players bring different kinds of fluency. One person may read a map quickly; another may pick up a shift in music or notice that a room’s objects tell a story. Some may be familiar with controller conventions, while others need time to learn what each button does. Resist turning those differences into a ranking. If the player gets stuck, ask whether they want a hint or would rather keep trying. If the observer spots a clue, ask before taking over. Pause when either person wants a break, and do not treat access settings as a compromise or a special favor. Sky LaRell Anderson analyzes how game lore and affective design can present historical learning through an interactive-museum-like experience [2]. At home, that means the person with the controller is not the only one who matters. Looking, listening, asking, and choosing when to pause are all ways of taking part.
Stop while there is still something to talk about

At the agreed stopping point, put the controller down before the conversation turns into a review of who played well. Each person can name one detail the other might have missed and one choice the game offered—or withheld. Then ask a question with more than one possible answer: “Which place felt most changed by what happened?” “Did the sound make you expect something?” “Would you have made the same choice?” Give the other person room to disagree or to say they are not sure. A good ending does not require a verdict on the game’s quality or a grand lesson about its message. If you want to continue another time, write down the scene or question you want to return to; if not, let the small experience be complete. The conversation is part of the play, but it does not need to become homework.
